# Windows: Respond (Incident Response)

Use with the core playbook, [incident-response.md](core/incident-response.md), which always
applies. This file adds only Windows-specific steps.

A compromised Windows PC usually means compromised accounts too: browser sessions, saved passwords,
email, the Microsoft account, and anything the PC can reach over the network (NAS shares, mapped drives,
other PCs with the same admin password). Plan to scope beyond the machine from the start.

## Triage and containment

- **Common home and small-office patterns:**
  - *Tech-support scam*: someone phoned, or a browser pop-up told the user to call; the user installed a
    remote-access tool or opened Quick Assist and let a stranger connect, and may have logged in to the
    bank while they watched.
  - *Ransomware*: ransom notes, files with new extensions, shadow copies deleted, Defender disabled,
    sometimes BitLocker enabled by the attacker with a key the owner doesn't have.
  - *Infostealer*: a cracked game or fake installer, followed by account takeovers elsewhere (email,
    social media, crypto wallets) even though the PC "seems fine".
  - *Exposed RDP*: successful external logons (event 4624 logon type 10) after many failures.
- **Disconnect the network, don't power off.** Unplug the Ethernet cable and turn off Wi-Fi (or enable
  airplane mode). Shutting down loses memory evidence and, if the attacker changed BitLocker protectors,
  may leave the owner unable to boot. Before any shutdown, confirm the owner can retrieve the BitLocker
  recovery key for this device. If ransomware is actively encrypting and the network can't be cut, a
  shutdown is acceptable: say so plainly.
- **Disconnect what the PC can reach:** unplug external backup drives; pause OneDrive and other sync
  clients only after checking pausing doesn't delete anything (pausing is safe; don't sign out or unlink
  if that would discard local changes); consider disconnecting mapped NAS shares at the NAS side.
- **Tell the user to act from a different, clean device** for account changes: change the Microsoft
  account password and sign out everywhere, then email, banking (call the bank if they shared banking
  details with a scammer), and password manager.
- **If an IT provider's RMM agent is on the machine**, ask whether the provider itself may be the source
  (supply-chain compromise of the provider's console is a known attack path) before trusting it for
  containment.

## Evidence to preserve (Windows-specific)

Collect before removing anything. Writing exports to the affected disk alters it; prefer an external
drive brought in for the purpose, and record hashes of exported files.

- **Event logs** (export with `wevtutil epl <log> <file>` to external media; never clear them):
  - Security: 4624/4625 (logons and failures, note logon type 3 network and 10 RDP), 4672 (admin logon),
    4720/4722/4732 (account created, enabled, added to a group), 4688 (process creation, if audited), 1102
    (log cleared).
  - System: 7045 (service installed), 104 (log cleared), unexpected restarts.
  - `Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational`: 1116/1117 (detections and actions), 5001 (real-time
    protection disabled), 5007 (configuration changed, including exclusions), 5013 (tamper protection
    blocked a change).
  - `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational` and `PowerShellCore/Operational`: 4104 (script blocks).
  - `Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational`: task registered, updated, run.
  - `Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-RemoteConnectionManager/Operational` (1149) and
    `...-LocalSessionManager/Operational` (21, 24, 25): RDP logons, disconnects, reconnects.
  - SMB server and client logs if shares were involved; `Microsoft-Windows-LAPS/Operational` in offices.
- **Defender state**: `Get-MpComputerStatus`, `Get-MpPreference` (exclusions, ASR, CFA state), and
  `Get-MpThreatDetection`; screenshots of Protection history.
- **Remote-access tools**: names, versions, install dates and paths, their services and tasks, their
  local log folders (most vendors keep connection logs with remote IDs and times), and the vendor account
  or session ID the user was given. Don't uninstall yet.
- **Persistence surfaces**: scheduled tasks (`Export-ScheduledTask` for suspicious ones), services with
  their `PathName`, Run/RunOnce keys, Startup folders, WMI subscriptions, browser extensions.
- **Accounts**: local users and group members, recently created or enabled accounts, `PasswordLastSet`.
- **Network**: listening ports and established connections with owning processes
  (`Get-NetTCPConnection`), firewall rules created recently, the hosts file, proxy settings, DNS
  settings.
- **Recovery state**: `vssadmin list shadows`, restore points, BitLocker status and protector **types and
  IDs** (never the recovery password). A protector you can't account for is evidence.
- **Ransomware**: one ransom note and a few sample encrypted files (copied, not moved), the new file
  extension, and timestamps of the earliest encrypted files.
- **Memory**: if the incident warrants it and a qualified responder is involved, a memory image before
  shutdown. Don't improvise memory capture with unknown tools.
- **Files of interest**: hash (`Get-FileHash`) and path of suspicious executables; don't run, move, or
  upload them to public scanners without the user's agreement (uploads can tip off the attacker and may
  contain personal data).

## Scope checks specific to Windows

- **The Microsoft account**: recent sign-in activity, new devices, changed recovery info, app passwords,
  OneDrive sharing links created, Outlook forwarding and inbox rules.
- **Browser data**: saved passwords and session cookies are what infostealers take. Treat every account
  saved in or signed in from any browser profile on the PC as exposed; sign out all sessions and change
  passwords from a clean device, starting with email and financial accounts.
- **Other PCs**: any machine sharing a local admin password with this one, any PC this user's account
  logs on to, and (in offices) the domain controller if a domain admin ever signed in to this PC.
- **Network storage**: NAS shares and mapped drives the PC could write to; check them for encryption or
  deletion and check their snapshots (see the NAS skill if one applies).
- **Remote-support vendor accounts**: if a legitimate tool was used, the vendor account may be
  compromised; check its device list and session history.
- **Work resources**: if the PC is used for work (VPN, email, a work-or-school account), notify the
  employer's IT or security team.
- **Financial exposure** in scam cases: bank, card, and payment accounts accessed during the session;
  advise contacting the bank directly using the number on the card.

## Domain controllers and Active Directory

If a domain admin account, a DC, a DC backup, or the hypervisor hosting a DC may be compromised, treat the
whole domain as compromised: every account, every domain-joined machine, and every system that trusts AD
for sign-in. This is specialist territory; bring in someone experienced with AD incident response early,
and use Microsoft's forest recovery guide.

- **Contain without destroying the domain.** Don't shut down or isolate the only DC unless the user
  accepts that nobody can sign in afterwards. Prefer cutting the DC's internet access and the attacker's
  remote paths (VPN, RDP forwards, remote-support tools) first. Disable, don't delete, accounts the
  attacker created or used, with fresh approval for each.
- **Evidence (DC-specific):** Security log events 4728/4732/4756 (members added to privileged groups),
  4720 (account created), 4724 (password reset by another account), 4738 (account changed), 4769
  (Kerberos service tickets, including RC4 requests that suggest Kerberoasting), 4662 (directory object
  access, including replication rights used by a non-DC), 5136/5137 (directory object modified or
  created, when directory service change auditing is on), and 4739 (domain policy changed); Directory
  Service and DFS Replication logs; `Get-GPO -All` modification times and a `Backup-GPO` copy of each GPO
  (to external media, with approval); privileged group membership with `whenChanged`; `AdminSDHolder`
  permissions; and the date of the last good system-state backup.
- **Scope**: every PC a compromised admin account signed in to, every server running a service as a
  domain account, the Entra Connect server if present (it can push changes to the cloud tenant), backup
  servers, and the hypervisor. Group Policy can deploy malware to every PC at once; check recently
  changed GPOs for scheduled tasks, scripts, or software installation.
- **Credential reset order** (plan it with the specialist, from a clean admin workstation): attacker
  access removed first; then all privileged accounts and break-glass accounts; then the **krbtgt
  password twice** (in a confirmed compromise, the specialist may choose a faster interval than the
  routine 10 hours and accept the disruption); then service accounts (gMSAs rotate on request), DSRM and
  LAPS passwords (rotate with `Reset-LapsPassword` on each machine or by expiring them in AD), and finally
  all user passwords. Resetting krbtgt only once leaves forged tickets usable.
- **Recovery from backup**: restore AD only from a backup taken before the earliest attacker activity,
  into an isolated network first, following Microsoft's forest recovery guide. Restoring a backup that
  already contains the attacker's accounts, GPOs, or persistence brings them back. A domain with one DC
  and no clean backup may need to be rebuilt; decide that with the user and the specialist, not alone.

## Eradication and recovery

- **Prefer a clean reinstall over cleanup** when an attacker had interactive or admin access, when
  ransomware ran, or when persistence is unclear. Use Microsoft's official installation media or "Reset
  this PC" with *Remove everything* and a cloud download, with the user present (this is C3 and a hard
  stop for automation). Back up the user's data first, and treat that backup as untrusted: scan it and
  never restore executables from it.
- A Defender full or offline scan finding nothing is not proof of safety (core section 6). Remote-access
  tools and stolen credentials are not malware detections.
- **Before reconnecting to the network**: Windows fully updated, Defender active with tamper protection on,
  firewall on, RDP off or VPN-only, no remote-access tools except approved ones, a standard daily account,
  BitLocker protection on with a **new** recovery password whose storage location is confirmed (the old
  one may have been seen), Windows Hello set up, and backups working to a location the PC can't delete.
- **Credentials**: Microsoft account password changed and all sessions signed out; two-step verification
  re-established on trusted devices; all browser-saved passwords rotated, starting with email; local admin
  passwords changed (rotate LAPS passwords in offices); Wi-Fi password changed if the attacker had admin
  access (stored keys are readable by admins).
- **Ransomware restores**: only from a backup taken before the earliest encryption, onto the cleaned or
  reinstalled system, and validated from a clean environment. OneDrive's file restore and version
  history can recover synced folders to an earlier point (availability depends on the plan; verify).
- After recovery, watch the Defender, Security, and RDP logs and the Microsoft account sign-in activity
  for several weeks.

## Quick checklist tailored for Windows

Start with the core quick checklist, plus:

- [ ] Disconnect Ethernet and Wi-Fi; don't shut down unless encryption is ongoing and you can't cut the
      network. Confirm the BitLocker recovery key is retrievable before any shutdown.
- [ ] Unplug external backup drives; pause sync clients.
- [ ] From a clean device: change the Microsoft account password, sign out everywhere, check two-step
      verification and recovery info; call the bank if financial details were shared.
- [ ] List remote-access tools, new accounts, Defender exclusions, and recent scheduled tasks; export the
      key event logs to external media.
- [ ] Plan a clean reinstall, a new BitLocker recovery password, and rotation of every password saved in
      the PC's browsers.
- [ ] Domain involved: bring in an AD specialist; preserve DC Security logs and GPO backups; plan the
      credential reset order, including krbtgt twice; restore AD only from a pre-compromise backup.
